Pathology of Blood Vessels II: Vasculitis and NeoplasmPTH LEC · LE 2 · Trans 4C · Socorro Cruz-Yañez MD

Overview

Whole-lesson summary

  • Vasculitis = inflammation of the blood vessels. Majority are immune mediated. Classified (CHCC) by the size of the vessel involved and the underlying etiology.
  • Diseases of veins: varicose veins and esophageal varices.
  • Diseases of lymphatics: lymphedema (primary and secondary/obstructive).
  • Tumors of blood vessels: benign (hemangioma, lymphangioma, glomus tumor) plus vascular ectasias, intermediate (Kaposi sarcoma), and malignant (angiosarcoma).

Must Know (red-exclamation points of this lecture)
  • GCA principally affects the arteries of the head and neck, particularly the temporal artery.
  • Over 50 years old: Giant cell arteritis. Under 50 years old: Takayasu arteritis.
  • Panarteritis nodosa has a MALE predilection.
  • Kawasaki disease: the coronary artery is the important affected vessel (neutrophils in all layers, intimal fibrinoid necrosis → thrombosis, aneurysm, rupture).
  • GPA: URT lesions range from inflammatory sinusitis to ulcerative lesions rimmed by granulomas with geographic central necrosis. Central to all features is granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels, often ANCA positive.
  • Buerger disease arteriogram: absence of flow of arterial dye toward the peripheral circulation.

I. Vasculitis: Definition, Mechanisms and Classification

Definition Must Know p. 1

  • Inflammation of the blood vessels
  • Vasculitis are a group of conditions characterized by inflammation and necrosis of the blood vessels
    • They are generally of unknown etiology
  • Any type of vessel can be affected
    • Small vessels like capillaries, venules, and arterioles
    • Large vessels like aorta
    • The type of vessel involved is important in the classification, as some types have predilections for certain types of blood vessels
  • Majority are immune mediated

Clinical manifestations p. 1

  • Vary and oftentimes involve multiple organs with systemic manifestations
    • Fever, arthralgia, myalgia, skin rashes, weight loss
  • May have acute exacerbations and spontaneous remissions
  • Some vasculitis lead to serious diseases that may require prompt recognition and treatment

Mechanisms Must Know p. 1

MechanismDetails
Direct injury to vessels
  • Caused by any infectious agents: virus, bacteria, fungi
  • Physical and chemical injury: radiation, mechanical trauma, toxin exposures
Immune-mediated inflammation
  • Cause of most forms of vasculitis are unknown
  • Majority of the underlying pathology is mediated by deposition of an Antigen-Antibody complex in the vessel wall
Ag-Ab complex deposits in vessel wall
→
Activation of the complement system
→
Acute inflammatory reaction in the blood vessel wall

Basis of classification p. 1

  • Size of the blood vessel involved
  • The underlying etiology
    • Known cause = secondary
    • None = primary

A. Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC)

Evolution of the classification p. 1–2

YearKey point
1994
  • Classification criteria formulated based on clinical presentation and the size of the blood vessel involved
  • Did not include ANCA and microscopic polyangiitis
2012
  • Updated with ancillary diagnostic procedures to include modern concepts of pathogenesis including ANCA
  • ANCA positive vs ANCA negative small vessel categories were incorporated here
2020LVV defined as vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches
Key Point
  • All three major categories of vasculitis (LVV, MVV, SVV) can affect any size of the artery.
  • The diagram depicts the usual distribution of vessel involvement.

Large vessel vasculitis (LVV)

  • Most often affects large arteries like the aorta
  • Defined as vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches
  • Two variants: Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis

Medium vessel vasculitis (MVV)

  • Predominantly affect medium sized arteries, but small arteries may be affected likewise
  • Two major categories
    • Polyarteritis nodosa: immune-complex mediated
    • Kawasaki disease: mediated by an anti-endothelial cell antibody

Small vessel vasculitis (SVV)

  • Predominantly affect venules, capillaries, and arterioles
  • Immune-complex small vessel vasculitis rarely affects the arteries
  • Subdivided into ANCA positive (ANCA-associated vasculitis, AAV) and ANCA negative (immune complex vasculitis)
SVV: ANCA positive
  • ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a necrotizing vasculitis with very few or no immune deposits, predominantly affecting small vessels, associated with MPO-ANCA or PR3-ANCA.
  • Important because ANCA specificity identifies distinct categories of the disease.
    • Microscopic polyangiitis
    • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): formerly Wegener's granulomatosis
    • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): formerly Churg Strauss Syndrome
SVV: ANCA negative
  • Immune-complex small vessel vasculitis: moderate to marked vessel wall deposits of immunoglobulin and complement, predominantly small vessels.
  • Glomerulonephritis is frequent.
    • Anti-GBM disease
    • Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis
    • IgA vasculitis (Henoch Schonlein Purpura)
    • Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis (anti-C1q vasculitis)
    • Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis

Table 1. CHCC framework for defining vasculitis Must Know p. 2

CHCC defines vasculitis according to the size of the vessels involved and the pattern of immune reaction in its underlying pathogenesis.

Classification based on pathogenesis

Vasculitis by pathogenesis p. 3
Direct infection
Direct damage of vessels by an organism or toxin
  • Tuberculosis
  • Fungus (Aspergillus)
  • Mucormycosis
Immunologic
Represents the vast majority of vasculitis, subclassified by mechanism:
  • Immune complex mediated: SLE, drug induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis
  • ANCA mediated: auto-Ab against neutrophils, endothelial cells, monocytes → Wegener's, microscopic PAN
  • Direct Ab attack: Goodpasture's (anti-GBM Ab affecting glomerular capillaries), Kawasaki's
  • Cell mediated: organ transplant rejection
  • Unknown or idiopathic: giant cell arteritis

B. ANCA-Associated Antibodies and Pathogenesis of Non-Infectious Vasculitis

ANCA: definition Must Know p. 2

  • Majority of vasculitis are immune-mediated: ANCA-antibody associated or immune complex type of reaction
  • ANCA are a group of auto-AB directed against azurophil or primary granules of PMN, lysosomes of monocytes, and endothelial cells
  • ANCA positive vasculitis: Wegener's granulomatosis, Microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome
  • Two patterns based on the immunofluorescent pattern, which provides the correct identification and subclassification of the vasculitis

c-ANCA vs p-ANCA Must Know p. 2–3

FeatureCytoplasmic (c-ANCA)Perinuclear (p-ANCA)
Major targetProteinase-3 (PR-3)Myeloperoxidase (MPO)
Current nameAnti-proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA)Anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA)
IF staining
  • Heavy staining in the cytoplasm
  • Non-reactive multilobulated nuclei (clear zone)
  • Staining limited to the perinuclear region
  • Non-reactive cytoplasm
Antigen notes
  • Neutrophil azurophilic granules
  • associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  • MPO is a lysosomal granule constituent involved in oxygen free radical generation
  • Induced by therapeutic agents, particularly propylthiouracil (PTU)
ExampleWegener granulomatosis (GPA)
  • Microscopic PAN
  • Churg-Strauss syndrome

Pathogenesis of non-infectious vasculitis

1. Immune complex p. 3

  • Ag-Ab complex deposited in the blood vessel wall → in-situ inflammatory reaction
  • e.g. serum sickness, SLE, Hep B, drug hypersensitivity

2. Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic AB (ANCA) Must Know p. 3

  • Heterogeneous group of auto-AB directed against constituents: mainly neutrophil primary granules, lysosomes, monocytes, and endothelial cells
  • Very useful diagnostic markers
    • Their titers generally mirror the clinical severity
    • A rise of titer is predictive of disease recurrence
  • Previously grouped by intracellular distribution (c-ANCA, p-ANCA), now classified according to their antigen specificity
  • Close association between ANCA titers and disease activity suggests a pathogenetic role
ANCA
→
Directly activate neutrophils
→
Release of reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes
→
Inflammatory interaction between inflammatory cells and endothelial cells

3. Anti-Endothelial Cell Ab p. 3

  • Directed against endothelial cells
  • Induced by defects in immune regulation, which can predispose to certain types of vasculitis
  • Categories: Kawasaki's Disease and Giant Cell (Temporal) arteritis
Clinical Cue: diagnosis of vasculitis
  • Requires a high index of suspicion, especially in the presence of multi-organ involvement.
  • Key to diagnosis is a detailed and systemic approach to patient assessment involving all potentially involved organs.
  • Tissue biopsy is helpful in establishing the diagnosis in order to provide the appropriate treatment.

C. Large Vessel Vasculitis

  • Inflammation of the blood vessel wall involving large arteries: aorta and its branches
  • Two prototypes: Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis (Giant Cell Aortitis)

Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis

Must KnowPrincipally affects the arteries in the head and neck, particularly the temporal artery.

Definition and epidemiology p. 3

  • Chronic, systemic inflammatory vasculitis involving large to small sized arteries, principally affects arteries in the head and neck
    • Also affects the ophthalmic, occipital, vertebral, posterior ciliary, and proximal vertebral arteries
  • Most common form of systemic vasculitis involving adults
    • Particularly elderly female
    • Rare before the age of 50

Etiology and pathogenesis p. 3

  • Cause is unknown, postulated to be of immunological origin
    • T cell-mediated immunologic response against vessel wall antigens
    • Anti-endothelial cell and anti-smooth muscle cell antibodies seen in 2/3rds of patients
    • Cellular immune etiology is supported by the characteristic granulomatous response in the vessel wall
  • Up to 50% of cases associated with polymyalgia rheumatica-like illness

Clinical features p. 3–4

  • Systemic / neurologic: headache, facial pain, scalp tenderness, myalgia, arthralgia
  • Ocular: blindness, blurring, eye pain Prev. trans
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica-like illness in up to 50%
  • The superficial temporal artery appears hard, tender, and pulseless, and the patient complains of severe headache
TreatmentAlmost all cases respond well to steroid therapy.

Morphology Must Know p. 4

AspectFeatures
Gross
  • Focal, segmental nodular thickening with normal intervening segments of the artery
  • Lesions only focally distributed, long segments of relatively normal artery may be interposed
Microscopic
  • Medial granuloma with giant cells
  • Fragmentation of internal elastic lamina (demonstrated by elastic stains)
  • Non-specific mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates: mostly CD4 and CD8 T cells with macrophages and multinucleated giant cells in 75% of specimens
Old / healed lesions
  • Fibrosis and thickening: intima and media become thickened and scarred, with residual elastic fragmentation and adventitial fibrosis
  • Thrombosis may occur
  • Fibrosis and intimal-medial thickening narrow and reduce the luminal diameter
  • Healed stage: medial attenuation and scarring with intimal thickening

Clinical diagnosis can often be confirmed by biopsy.

Takayasu Arteritis

Definition and distribution p. 5

  • Rare granulomatous vasculitis that involves the medium and larger arteries like the aorta
    • Commonly involves the aorta, aortic arch, and its great vessel branches → the so-called "Aortic Arch Syndrome"
    • In 10-15%: carotid, subclavian, coronary, and pulmonary arteries may be involved
  • Characterized by ocular disturbances and marked weakening of the pulses in the upper extremities → "pulseless disease"
  • Most patients are young to middle aged (<40 years old) and female, presenting with hypertension or ischemic symptoms in the arms
    • Global distribution, traditionally associated with the Japanese population
  • Renal arterial involvement can cause hypertension
  • Manifests with transmural fibrous thickening of the aorta, particularly the aortic arch and great vessels, with severe luminal narrowing of the major aortic branches
  • Pathogenesis: unknown, postulated autoimmune etiology
Must Know · Key Differentiator: Takayasu vs GCA
  • Shares many morphologic attributes with GCA, including clinical features and histomorphology.
  • Distinction is based on the age of the patient:
  • Over 50 years old: Giant cell arteritis / temporal arteritis
  • Under 50 years old: Takayasu aortitis / arteritis
  • Takayasu's arteritis: affects adolescent girls and young women (≤40 years old), especially among Asians.
  • Giant cell arteritis: occurs in older individuals and is rarely seen below 40 years of age.

Clinical presentation p. 5

  • Ocular disturbance
    • Visual defects, retinal detachment, blindness
    • Reflects involvement of ophthalmic arteries
  • Pulseless disease (upper extremities)
    • HPN, neurologic defects
    • Marked difference in pulses of upper and lower extremities
      • Upper limbs: loss of pulse and reduction of blood pressure
      • Lower limbs: normal to bounding pulses
    • Arm claudication, pulselessness, discrepant blood pressures, and bruits
    • Hypertension may follow if the renal artery is involved

Treatment and prognosis p. 5

  • Only a proportion of patients respond to treatment (steroids or other agents)
  • Outlook is much worse than in GCA
  • Few patients make a complete recovery
  • Associated hypertension may be difficult to control

Morphology p. 5

AspectFeatures
Gross
  • Affected vessel thick and fibrotic
  • with aortic wall thickening and narrowing of the lumen
Histologic
  • Adventitial and medial mononuclear inflammation
  • Perivascular cuffing
  • Chronic granulomatous vasculitis with multinucleated giant cells, with complications of fibrosis, stenosis, occlusion, and occasionally aneurysmal dilatation
  • Medial arterial wall necrosis
Exam TrapDiagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires correlation with the clinical features, because the histologic pattern may be confused with GCA.

D. Medium Size Vessel Arteritis

  • Inflammation of the medium-sized vessel
  • Two prototypes: Panarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki's vasculitis

Panarteritis (Polyarteritis) Nodosa

Must KnowPAN has a MALE predilection.

Definition and epidemiology p. 6

  • Rare vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized muscular arteries but spares the pulmonary arteries
  • Primarily a disease of young adults, but can occur in all age groups
  • Cause remains unknown in the majority of cases

Forms p. 6

Systemic formCutaneous form
  • Affects the kidneys, liver, GIT, and the nervous system
  • Skin involvement in 10% of cases
  • Mild constitutional symptoms, little systemic involvement
  • More favorable prognosis, but runs a chronic relapsing and remitting course
  • Tender papules and plaques, purpuric livedo reticularis, skin necrosis, ulceration
Key Differentiator: PAN and ANCA / Hepatitis B
  • No association with ANCA.
  • 1/3rd of patients have chronic Hepatitis B (30% of cases) → HBsAg-HBsAb complex deposits on affected vessels.

Clinical course and signs p. 6–7

  • Clinical manifestations result from ischemia and infarction of affected tissues and organs
  • Course is frequently remitting and episodic with long symptom-free intervals
  • Widely scattered vascular involvement → variable signs and symptoms
    • Fever of unknown origin
    • Rapidly accelerating hypertension
    • Abdominal pain and bloody stool (vascular GIT lesions), diffuse myalgia, peripheral neuropathies
    • Peripheral neuritis
    • Hemorrhagic maculopapular rashes with skin ulcerations
  • Untreated: typically fatal
  • Immunosuppression → remission or cure in 90%

Morphology Must Know p. 7

  • Involved arteries show sharp segmental distribution with nodular thickening
  • Biopsy shows arterial involvement displaying variable stages of morphological development
    • Key feature that differentiates it from microscopic polyangiitis or leukocytoclastic vasculitis
  • Impaired perfusion distal to the lesion → ulceration, infarcts, ischemic atrophy, or hemorrhage
Three histological stages
Acute
  • Intimal fibrinoid necrosis
  • Transmural inflammation (intima, media, adventitia) → "panarteritis"
  • Neutrophils with few eosinophils and lymphocytes
  • Complication: aneurysm (weakened wall)
→
Healing
  • Granulation tissue and fibro-reparative process
  • Mononuclear cells, chiefly lymphocytes
  • Fibrous thickening may occlude the lumen
→
Healed (fibrotic)
  • Marked fibrosis with minimal inflammation Prev. trans
  • Firm nodular scars of the affected artery

Kawasaki Syndrome / Disease

Definition p. 7

  • Affects large and medium sized arteries, associated with mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome
    • Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome: enlarged, tender, painful lymph nodes, particularly on the posterior cervical angle Lecturer
    • Mucocutaneous symptoms Lecturer: ulcer, red, chapped/cracked lips, conjunctivitis, skin lesions (palmar erythema)
  • Acute febrile illness of early childhood: young children, infants, Asians (boys > girls)
    • Higher incidence in Asians thought to be linked to genetic susceptibility
    • 80% of patients are <4 years of age
  • Syndrome of unknown cause
Must Know: coronary artery involvement
  • Predilection for the coronary arteries with potential for coronary artery aneurysm.
  • Signs of ischemic heart disease and acute myocardial infarction in children may be observed.
  • Long-standing vasculitis → dilatation and aneurysm of the coronary artery → rupture and hemorrhage.
  • Heart complications are the most important aspect of Kawasaki's disease.
  • Leading cause of heart disease acquired in childhood in the US and Japan.

Signs, symptoms and clinical presentation p. 7–8

  • Fever, erythema
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy (acute febrile episode, usually self-limited)
  • Mucocutaneous desquamative erythematous rashes involving the mouth, genital areas, eyes, palms, soles, and skin
    • Erythematous, red, maculopapular lesions that desquamate and peel off, can involve the soles and palms
  • CVS symptoms: ring aneurysmal dilation of the coronary arteries on X-ray

Pathogenesis p. 8

Trigger from infection, usually viral Lecturer
→
Inappropriate immunologic response in genetically predisposed children
→
T-cell and macrophage activation, cytokine secretion
→
Formation of auto-AB vs ECs and SMCs
  • Specific cause is unknown
  • Vasculitis may result from a delayed type hypersensitivity response directed against cross-reactive or newly uncovered vascular antigens

Morphology p. 8

  • Segmental, necrotizing, fibrinoid panarteritis of the involved artery
  • Early stages: dense transmural inflammatory infiltrate involving all layers, with some intimal fibrinoid necrosis
  • Elastic stain: intimal-medial thickening and disruption of internal and external elastic lamina
  • Acute vasculitis typically subsides spontaneously or with treatment, but aneurysm formation due to wall damage can occur
  • Healed lesions can exhibit obstructive intimal thickening

E. Small Vessel Vasculitis (Part I)

Overview of small vessel vasculitis p. 9

  • Tend to be polyangiitis involving arterioles, venules, and capillaries
ANCA Associated VasculitisImmune Complex Vasculitis
  • Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) (GPA)
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) (EGPA)
  • Anti-GBM disease
  • Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (CV)
  • IgA vasculitis / Henoch-Schonlein (IgAV)

Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) aka Wegener Granulomatosis

Definition p. 9

  • Rare and long term systemic disorder involving the formation of granulomas and vasculitis
  • Small vessel vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized vessels in many organs, more commonly the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys
  • Signs and symptoms are varied and reflect the organ involved

Triad Must Know p. 9

  1. Acute necrotizing granulomas of the upper RT (ear, nose, sinuses, throat) and/or lower RT (lung, bronchus) → sinusitis, ulcers, and cavitations
    • Upper airway + lower airway manifestations of the lungs, leading to cavitary lesions, infiltrates Lecturer
  2. Focal necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis of small- and medium-sized vessels, prominent in the lungs and upper airways
  3. Proliferative or crescentic glomerulonephritis / Rapidly Progressive GN (RPGN)
    • Focal necrotizing, often crescentic GN
    • Can lead to acute renal failure
Must Know
  • URT lesions range from inflammatory sinusitis with mucosal granulomas to ulcerative lesions of the nose, palate, or pharynx, rimmed by granulomas with geographic patterns of central necrosis and vasculitis.
  • Central to all clinical features: presence of granulomatous vasculitis involving small blood vessels and often ANCA positive.

Clinical features p. 9

SiteFeatures
Multi-organFever
LRTCavitations, nodules, hemoptysis
URT
  • Saddle nose
  • Necrotizing granulomas surrounded by a zone of proliferative fibroblasts with giant cells and leukocytic infiltrate (reminiscent of TB)
  • Multiple granulomas may coalesce → radiographically visible nodules that can cavitate
  • Late stages: progressive fibrosis and organization
  • Central to the lesion: focal necrotizing granulomas of small and medium vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) → "polyangiitis" → ischemic necrosis of surrounding tissue
RenalSegmental and focal necrotizing GN with crescents, hematuria, ARF
  • Mild: focal glomerular necrosis with isolated capillary loop thrombosis
  • Advanced: diffuse necrosis and parietal proliferation → crescents
Others
  • Myalgias
  • arthralgia
  • neuritis
  • skin rashes

Pathogenesis p. 9

  • T-cell mediated hypersensitivity immune response
    • Initiator/trigger: inhaled microbial organism (S. aureus) or environmental agent
  • Genetic predisposition: HLA, CTLA4
    • Supported by the presence of granulomas and response to immunosuppressive treatment
  • 95% positive with c-ANCA / PR3-ANCA
    • Useful marker for disease activity and may participate in pathogenesis
    • Typical ANCAs react with proteinase 3 (enzyme prevalent in neutrophils)
  • Responds to immunosuppression
  • Males are affected more than females Lecturer
Exam Trap · Lecture-Specific Note
  • In the synchronous formative quiz (35/F, nasal and oral lesions, proteinuria, hematuria), the answer was Wegener's granulomatosis with a positive P-ANCA.
  • Trans note: should be c-ANCA positive according to Robbins, but the lecturer said p-ANCA.

Morphology p. 9

  • Lesions primarily of blood vessels with granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tract and kidneys
  • Necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of small arteries and venules with granuloma formation
  • Lung: multiple bilateral cavitary infiltrates
  • Upper airway: sinus and NP inflammation, necrosis, granuloma formation, vasculitis
  • Kidneys: focal and segmental GN → Rapidly Progressive (crescentic) GN
High-Yield Recap · Lecturer emphasisGranulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells is also seen in temporal arteritis, Kawasaki's, and Wegener's granulomatosis.

Thromboangiitis Obliterans (Buerger's Disease)

Definition and epidemiology p. 10

  • An inflammatory vasculopathy: inflammation and arteritis cause a prothrombotic state, forming a thrombotic vasoocclusive phenomenon
    • Inflammatory process is initiated within the tunica intima
  • Segmental, thrombosing, acute and chronic inflammation of medium and small arteries, occasionally veins and nerves
  • Associated with a strong history of heavy cigarette smoking
  • Usually common among young males (<35 yrs old)
Segmental thrombosing inflammation
→
Thrombotic occlusion
→
Peripheral gangrene of fingers and toes
→
Progressive changes → serial amputations

Etio-pathogenesis p. 10

  • Unknown etiology
  • Use or exposure to tobacco triggers immune response and vasculitis
    • In susceptible persons, or it may unmask a clotting defect → vasculitis and ischemic changes in the distal limbs
  • Tobacco products trigger either a direct idiosyncratic EC toxicity or an immune response against vascular wall proteins
  • Most patients have hypersensitivity to intradermally injected tobacco extracts

Morphology Must Know p. 11

  • Focal acute and chronic vasculitis of small and medium sized arteries
  • Acute and chronic inflammation with luminal thrombosis (thrombus may recanalize)
  • Microabscess in the thrombus surrounded by granulomatous inflammation
  • Late stage: intimal fibrosis, thrombus organization, and peri-arteritis
    • Inflammation extends into contiguous veins and nerves → encased in fibrous tissue

Clinical features p. 10–11

  • Granulomatous vasculitis that tends to be occlusive due to thrombus formation with abscess → distal digit gangrene requiring amputation
  • Fibrosis eventually encases the neurovascular bundles, transmural inflammation
  • Pain is an important feature due to neural involvement
  • Cold induced Raynaud phenomenon (impaired circulation increases sensitivity to cold)
  • Leg pain, intermittent claudication
  • Diminished to absent peripheral pulses, ulcers, gangrene → amputation
If you see X, think Y (formative quiz)30-year-old male smoker with gangrene of the extremities → biopsy most suggestive of Buerger's: thrombosis with micro abscesses.

E. Small Vessel Vasculitis (Part II)

Microscopic Polyangiitis (Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis)

Definition p. 11

  • AKA: Hypersensitivity vasculitis, microscopic PAN
  • Small vessels: arterioles, capillaries, venules
    • Predilection for skin, with less involvement of visceral organs (mucous membranes, lungs, brain, heart, GIT, kidneys, muscle)
    • In 90% of cases, necrotizing glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis are common
  • Immune mediated
    • Can be a feature of many immune disorders like Henoch-Schonlein purpura or vasculitis of connective tissue disorders like SLE
  • MPO-ANCA positive in the majority of cases
Must Know · Key Differentiator
  • MPA lesions tend to be of the same age in any given patient → suggests a single episode of antibody or immune complex deposition.
  • All lesions of same histologic age, with fibrinoid necrosis and transmural inflammation.

Pathogenesis p. 12

Antibody response to antigens: drugs (Penicillin), microorganisms (Streptococci), heterologous proteins, tumor proteins
→
Immune complex deposition or secondary immune responses (e.g. develop ANCAs) that are pathogenic
→
Segmental fibrinoid necrosis of media with focal transmural necrotizing lesions

In-lesson comparison: MPA vs PAN p. 7, 12

FeatureMicroscopic polyangiitisPanarteritis nodosa

  • infarcts

Churg-Strauss Syndrome (EGPA): Eosinophilic Granulomatous Polyangiitis

Definition p. 12

  • AKA: Allergic Granulomatosis Polyangiitis
  • Small vessel necrotizing granulomatous eosinophilic polyangiitis
    • Eosinophilic infiltration of the capillaries, venules, and arterioles
  • Associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis, prominent peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, extravascular granuloma, multi-organ vasculitis, and cardiomyopathy
  • MPO-ANCA positivity

Clinical presentation p. 12

FeatureDetails
Key featureNecrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, venules) with eosinophilic infiltrates
Constitutional
  • Fever
  • malaise
  • anorexia
  • weight loss
URT and LRTAllergic rhinitis, sinusitis, asthmatic attacks with lung infiltrates
NervesMononeuritis multiplex in 70%
Skin
  • Purpura
  • cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules
Kidney
  • Focal segmental GS → hematuria
  • proteinuria

Microscopic features p. 12

  • Central: eosinophilic granulomatous polyangiitis of small vessels
  • Radially arranged histiocytes and palisading multinucleated giant cells near small vessels
  • +/- sarcoid-like granulomas, focal fibrosis, and eosinophilic microabscesses

Infectious Vasculitis

  • Arteritis caused by direct invasion of infectious agents into the blood vessel wall
    • Bacteria: Pseudomonas
    • Fungi: Aspergillus and Mucor spp.
    • May be due to direct continuous spread from local tissue infection
  • Complications: mycotic aneurysm, thrombosis, and infarction
High-Yield Recap: Vasculitis Key Facts
  • Definition: inflammation of vessel walls.
  • Etiopathogenesis: majority are immune mediated through immune complex deposition, antibodies like ANCAs, or anti-EC/SMC Ab. Direct wall injury (less common) via toxins or infectious agents.
  • S/S: varied, with constitutional presentation and specific target organ dysfunction.
  • Classification (CHCC): reflects preferential anatomical distribution while incorporating antibody diagnostic schemes: large, medium, and small vessel (tends to be polyvascular).
  • Each vasculitis has unique features, but with significant overlap in morphologic features.

II. Disease of Veins and III. Disease of Lymphatics

The peripheral and internal venous system returns deoxygenated blood to the general circulation via the superior or inferior vena cava.

Varicose Veins (Varicosities)

Definition Must Know p. 13

  • Abnormal dilatation and tortuosity of veins
Causes (prolonged increase in pressure and weakening)
  1. Increased intraluminal pressure → vessel dilation: prolonged standing, intra-abdominal pressure, portal hypertension
  2. Venous valve incompetence
  3. Loss of vessel support → vein weakening
  • Superficial veins of the upper and lower legs are commonly involved (venous pressure, posture)
  • Obesity increases the risk, with a familial predisposition (defective venous wall development)
  • Can occur in other organs: esophagus (portal hypertension from liver cirrhosis) and anal hemorrhoids
Complications
  • Stasis dermatitis and ulcers.
  • Thrombosis.
  • Hemorrhage.
  • Superimposed infections.
  • Life-threatening hemorrhage in esophageal varices.
  • Embolism (rare).

Esophageal Varices

  • Increased portal hypertension induces dilation of the esophageal venous plexuses
  • Complication: potentially fatal gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Microscopic: partially dilated and thickened venous channel with an intraluminal thrombus

Diseases of Lymphatics

  • Primary disorders of lymphatic vessels are extremely uncommon
  • Secondary processes frequently develop with inflammation or malignancies

Lymphedema: due to lymphatic obstruction p. 13

CauseExamples
Congenital
  • Milroy disease: hereditary lymphedema due to absence of lymphatics
  • autosomal dominant
Infectious
  • Schistosomiasis
  • lymphangitis
Obstructive
  • Cancer metastasis
  • surgical manipulation and dissection
  • removal of lymph nodes
TraumaticSprain
IdiopathicLymphedema praecox

Secondary / Obstructive Lymphedema p. 13

  • Stems from blockage of previously normal lymphatics
  • W. bancrofti (Filariasis or Elephantiasis) inhabits the inguinal lymph node → chronic inflammation with fibrosis → lymphedema
  • Also seen in tumors obstructing regional lymph nodes and surgery like mastectomy (removal of draining lymphatics for breast carcinoma)

IV. Tumors of Blood Vessels

General points p. 14

  • Tumors of blood vessels have vascular origins: from blood vessels or lymphatic channels
  • Classified into: Benign, Intermediate, Malignant
  • Vascular neoplasms arise from either:
    • The endothelium (e.g. hemangioma, lymphangioma, angiosarcoma)
    • Cells that support the surrounding blood vessels (e.g. Glomus tumor)
  • Primary tumors of large vessels (aorta, pulmonary artery and veins) are mostly sarcomas
  • Congenital or developmental malformations and non-neoplastic reactive vascular proliferations (e.g. bacillary angiomatosis) can present as tumor-like lesions

Figure 30. Classification of vascular tumors and tumor-like conditions Must Know p. 14

CategoryEntities
Benign neoplasms, developmental and acquired conditions
  • Hemangioma: capillary hemangioma, cavernous hemangioma, pyogenic granuloma
  • Lymphangioma: simple (capillary) lymphangioma, cavernous lymphangioma (cystic hygroma)
  • Glomus tumor
  • Vascular ectasias: nevus flammeus, spider telangiectasia (arterial spider), hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease)
  • Reactive vascular proliferations: bacillary angiomatosis
Intermediate-grade neoplasms
  • Kaposi sarcoma
  • Hemangioendothelioma
Malignant neoplasms
  • Angiosarcoma
  • Hemangiopericytoma

Hemangioma

General p. 14

  • Most common vascular tumor of small capillaries
  • 7% of all benign tumors in infancy and childhood
  • Most are present at birth and may regress spontaneously
  • Common in the head and neck, thoracic skin, or liver (visceral hemangioma)
  • If extensive → angiomatosis
  • Rarely malignant
  • Morphologic variants: capillary hemangioma, cavernous hemangioma, pyogenic granuloma

Capillary hemangioma p. 14

  • Most common benign soft tissue tumor
  • Sites: skin, subcutaneous tissue, mucous membranes of oral cavity and lips
    • Also liver, spleen, kidneys
  • "Strawberry tumor" (juvenile hemangioma): in children and infants, red, fleshy, succulent mass resembling strawberries
  • Rapidly grow but spontaneously regress in 75-90% at ages 1-3 years, completely regressed by 7 years
  • Gross: bright red to blue, flat, elevated or pedunculated
  • Histologic
    • Benign, lobular proliferation of closely packed thin-walled blood filled capillaries
    • Scant intervening stroma
    • Lined by flattened, benign endothelial cells
    • Secondary complications: thrombosis, bleeding, infection

Cavernous hemangioma p. 14–15

  • Less common, larger, deeply situated
  • Benign proliferation of large dilated vascular channels
  • More infiltrative, frequently involves deep structures
  • Difficult to distinguish from malignant counterparts
  • No regression
  • One component of von Hippel-Lindau disease (systemic hemangiomas in cerebellum, brain stem, eye, pancreas, liver)
  • Histology: sharply delineated but unencapsulated, large blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma
    • Intravascular thrombosis with dystrophic calcification is common, can be locally destructive or infiltrative
  • Hemangiomas can cause bleeding and may be fatal if in the brain

Pyogenic granuloma (Lobular capillary hemangioma) p. 15

  • The most common type of reactive, proliferative tumor
    • Grows in response to stimuli such as stromal or local thrombus
    • Can form in pregnancy as a hormonal reaction
  • Rapid growth, fleshy, red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, and oral mucosa
  • Bleed easily and are often ulcerated
  • ⅓ develop after trauma, size 1-2 cm within a few weeks
  • Inflamed stromal vessels resembling granulation tissue, with acute and chronic inflammation
  • Spontaneously regress
  • Granuloma gravidarum: gingiva of pregnant women
    • Regresses after delivery and undergoes fibrosis
    • Occasionally requires surgical excision

Lymphangioma

Lymphangioma p. 15

  • Benign tumor of lymphatics
  • Most located superficially in the subcutaneous tissues of the head, neck and axilla
  • Nodule filled with milky fluid
  • Benign proliferations of endothelium-lined lymph spaces, without blood cells
    • Some filled with proteinaceous milky fluid
  • Cystic hygroma: variant, large cystic lymphangioma

Cystic hygroma / cystic lymphangioma p. 15

AspectFeatures
Gross
  • Large, unencapsulated tumors with large cystic spaces containing milky fluid
  • Typically in the neck and axilla of children
  • Can grow enormously
Microscopic
  • Large lymphatic channels lined by a single layer of endothelial cells
  • Loose connective tissue stroma with lymphoid aggregates
  • Channels devoid of red blood cells

Glomus Tumor / Glomangioma

Glomus tumor p. 15–16

  • Benign, very painful tumor
  • Commonly in the finger or beneath the nail bed
  • Origin: modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body (arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation)
  • Small, round, red-blue nodules, subungual location
  • Excision is curative
  • Gross: well-circumscribed, fleshy masses
  • Microscopic
    • Glomus cells (neoplastic component): nests and sheets in a myxoid stroma
      • Round, sharply punched-out nuclei with pink or amphophilic cytoplasm
      • Round, uniform, indistinct margins
    • Vasculature: branching, capillary-sized vessels
    • Endothelial cells line the vasculature

Vascular Ectasias

Terms p. 16

  • Ectasia: any local dilation of a structure
  • Telangiectasia: a permanent dilation of pre-existing vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), typically in the skin → discrete red lesion
  • Not a true tumor / neoplasm
  • Can be congenital or acquired
  • Types: Nevus flammeus, Spider telangiectasia (arterial spider), Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease)

Nevus Flammeus

Nevus flammeus (Birthmark, Port wine nevus) p. 16

  • Most common form of vascular ectasia
  • Flat, light pink to purple lesions with discrete borders on the head and neck
    • Composed of dilated vessels, can appear map-like
    • May grow proportionately with the child and thicken the skin surface
  • The majority regress and can fade away or persist through life
  • Microscopic: non-neoplastic, dilated small channels in the dermis
  • Those along the trigeminal nerve are associated with Sturge-Weber Syndrome

Port wine stain and Sturge-Weber Syndrome Must Know p. 16–17

  • Port wine stain: a special form of nevus flammeus, rare congenital disorder
    • Tends to grow during childhood and persist over time, with thickening of the skin surface
    • Distribution along the trigeminal nerve
  • Sturge-Weber Syndrome (Encephalo-trigeminal angiomatosis): rare congenital disorder
    • Venous angiomatosis in the leptomeninges and cortex
    • Ipsilateral port wine nevi of the face
    • Intellectual disability (mental retardation), seizures
    • Hemiplegia, radiopacities in the skull
Clinical Cue
  • A large facial telangiectasia in a child with intellectual deficiency indicates additional vascular malformations.
  • Formative quiz: child with delayed mental development, red-purplish map-like birthmark of one side of the face, and angiomas on CT → Sturge-Weber Syndrome.

Spider Telangiectasia

Spider telangiectasia (Arterial spider) p. 17

  • Non-neoplastic malformation resembling a spider
  • Radial, pulsatile network of dilated subcutaneous arteries or arterioles (spider legs) around a central core (spider body)
    • Usually blanches on pressure
  • Does not cause symptoms or complications
  • Usual location: face, neck, or upper chest
  • Seen in pregnancy and liver cirrhosis
    • Associated with hyperestrogenic states (hyperestrinism plays a role)

Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia

HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu Disease) p. 17

  • Genetically predetermined: autosomal dominant
    • Mutations in genes encoding components of the TGF-β signaling pathway in endothelial cells
  • Dilated capillaries and veins present at birth
  • Widely distributed: skin, mucous membranes of the oral cavity, lips, respiratory, GIT, and urinary tract
  • Lesions can spontaneously rupture → serious epistaxis, GI bleeding, or hematuria

V. Intermediate Malignancy and Malignant Tumor

Kaposi Sarcoma (Intermediate)

General Must Know p. 17

  • Most common AIDS associated cancer
  • Present in ⅓ of AIDS
  • Caused by HHV 8 (Human Herpes Virus 8)
  • 4 variants
    1. Chronic (Classic or European KS)
    2. Lymphadenopathic (African / Endemic KS)
    3. Transplant-associated (immunosuppression-associated KS)
    4. AIDS associated (Epidemic KS)

Pathogenesis p. 17–18

  • 95% of HIV patients with KS lesions have HHV-8 / KSHV (Kaposi Sarcoma associated Herpesvirus)
  • Transmitted sexually and potentially by oral secretions and cutaneous exposure
  • HHV-8 together with altered T-cell immunity are co-factors (cofactor of immunosuppression)
HHV-8 causes latent infection of endothelial cells
→
Induces VEGF production → stimulates endothelial growth
→
Viral proteins inhibit p53 and produce a viral homologue of cyclin D
→
Disrupted control of proliferation + prevented apoptosis of endothelial cells

Local inflammatory environmental factors of cellular proliferation are also stimulated.

1. Chronic / Classic / European KS p. 18

  • Seen (90%) in older men of Eastern EU (especially Ashkenazi Jews) or Mediterranean descent
  • Indolent, slow-growing, single or multiple erythematous patches on the lower extremities
  • Multiple red to purple skin plaques/nodules in the arms or legs
  • Good prognosis
    • Well-functioning immune system
    • Persistent but asymptomatic, localized to skin and subcutaneous tissue
  • Not associated with HIV (but can be associated with malignancy or altered immunity)
  • 10% visceral involvement

2. Lymphadenopathic / African / Endemic KS p. 18

  • Sub-Saharan Africa, South Africa, young Bantu children
  • Involves lymph nodes more frequently than classic → local or generalized lymphadenopathy, skin lesions sparse
    • Can also present with a cutaneous form
  • Not related to HIV
  • Aggressive, poor clinical course
  • Risk factors: Sub-Saharan Africans, chronic malaria, chronic parasitic infection, malnutrition
  • Poor prognosis with lymph node and visceral involvement: 100% mortality in 3 years

3. Transplant-associated KS (Immunosuppression-associated, Iatrogenic) p. 18

  • Occurs in solid organ transplant recipients on high doses of immunosuppressive treatment
  • Triggered by immunosuppression: any individual with weak immunity, irrespective of age, race, ethnicity, both genders equally
  • Not related to HIV
  • Aggressive: involves lymph nodes, mucosa, and visceral organs
  • Cutaneous lesions may be absent
  • Lesions can regress as immunosuppression is reduced
  • Risk factors: immunosuppressive medications post-transplant, chemotherapy, severely weakened immunity

4. AIDS associated / Epidemic KS p. 19

  • Most common HIV-related malignancy
  • Aggressive, often involves skin and LN, disseminates widely to visceral organs early
  • Metastasis occurs early
  • Most aggressive form of Kaposi sarcoma
  • Mortality due to opportunistic infections
  • Purplish red patches mainly in the legs, hands, and face
    • Multiple red-purple macules of varying sizes that become larger with raised plaque edges
  • Risk factors: HIV infection, transfusion of HIV-containing blood, sharing contaminated needles

Clinical features of KS p. 19

  • Skin lesions: 3 stages (multiple red, purple patch, plaque, and macules in skin and mucosa)
  • Lymph node infiltration: enlarged and infiltrated, particularly in lymphadenopathic KS
  • Visceral involvement (liver, spleen, mucosa): more aggressive clinical course
Histology
  • Nodular proliferation of dilated irregular endothelial cell-lined vascular spaces with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages (sometimes with hemosiderin)
    • Can be difficult to distinguish from granulation tissue
  • Dilated, jagged vascular channels lined and surrounded by plump atypical spindle cells
  • Between channels: extravasated erythrocytes, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, mononuclear cells
  • Progression → cellular sheets of atypical spindle cells with slit-like spaces containing red cells and hemorrhage

Angiosarcoma (Malignant)

Definition p. 20

  • Malignant endothelial neoplasm, histology ranging from highly differentiated tumors resembling hemangiomas to profoundly anaplastic highly cellular lesions
  • Adult, malignant vascular tumor, commonly older adults, male and female
  • Sites: skin, soft tissue, breast, liver, can occur in any site
  • Clinical behavior: aggressive, metastasis, poor outcome

Etiogenesis Must Know p. 20

AgentDetails
Carcinogens
  • Arsenic (in pesticides)
  • Thorotrast (radioactive contrast agent)
  • Polyvinyl chloride (one of the best known human chemical carcinogens)
Chronic lymphedemaLymphangiosarcoma: post-mastectomy or post-radiation
Radiation—
Foreign bodyProsthetic devices inserted for a prolonged time

All agents have long latencies between initial exposure and tumor development.

Morphology p. 20

AspectFeatures
Gross
  • Multiple red papules or nodules on the skin
  • Multiple large, fleshy, hemorrhagic nodules in viscera
  • Necrosis and hemorrhage are common
Histologic
  • All degrees of differentiation: from plump atypical endothelial cells forming irregular channels to highly cellular undifferentiated tumors with no discernible vessels
  • Atypical vascular spaces lined by endothelial cells with cytologic atypia and multilayering
Endothelial originImmunohistochemistry for CD31 or vWF (endothelial cell markers)

Cram Sheet

Red-exclamation must-knows
  • GCA: head and neck arteries, particularly the temporal artery.
  • Over 50 years old → GCA. Under 50 years old → Takayasu.
  • Takayasu: adolescent girls and young women (≤40), especially Asians. GCA: older individuals, rarely below 40.
  • PAN: MALE predilection.
  • Kawasaki (Fig 16): coronary artery diffusely infiltrated (adventitia, media, intima) by abundant neutrophils, intima with dense pink fibrinoid necrosis → coronary thrombosis, aneurysm, or rupture.
  • GPA: URT lesions range from inflammatory sinusitis with mucosal granulomas to ulcerative lesions of nose, palate, pharynx, rimmed by granulomas with geographic central necrosis and vasculitis.
  • GPA: central to all features is granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels, often ANCA positive.
  • Buerger arteriogram: absence of flow of arterial dye toward the periphery = obstruction.

Core definitions

  • Vasculitis: inflammation of the blood vessels (inflammation and necrosis), majority immune mediated
    • Mechanisms: direct injury (infection, physical/chemical) vs immune-mediated (Ag-Ab complex → complement → acute inflammation)
    • Classified by vessel size and etiology (secondary = known cause, primary = none)
  • ANCA: auto-Ab against azurophil/primary granules of PMN, lysosomes of monocytes, and endothelial cells
    • Titers mirror clinical severity, rising titer predicts recurrence
    • ANCA → activate neutrophils → ROS + proteolytic enzymes → endothelial injury
  • Varicose veins: abnormal dilatation and tortuosity of veins (↑ intraluminal pressure, valve incompetence, loss of support)
  • Lymphedema: due to lymphatic obstruction (Milroy = congenital AD absence of lymphatics, W. bancrofti = elephantiasis)
  • Telangiectasia: permanent dilation of pre-existing small vessels, not a true neoplasm
Classification anchors
Large
  • GCA
  • Takayasu (granulomatous)
Medium
  • PAN (immune complex)
  • Kawasaki (anti-EC Ab)
Small ANCA +
  • MPA
  • GPA
  • EGPA (few/no immune deposits)
Small ANCA −
  • Anti-GBM
  • cryoglobulinemic
  • IgA (HSP)
  • anti-C1q
  • cutaneous leukocytoclastic (GN frequent)
By pathogenesis
  • Immune complex: SLE, drug leukocytoclastic
  • ANCA: Wegener, MPA
  • Direct Ab: Goodpasture, Kawasaki
  • Cell mediated: transplant rejection
  • Idiopathic: GCA

Key values
GCA
  • PMR-like illness up to 50%
  • anti-EC/SMC Ab in 2/3
  • giant cells in 75%
  • rare before 50
Takayasu
  • <40 yrs
  • other arteries in 10-15%
PAN
  • Skin 10%
  • Hep B 1/3 (30%)
  • immunosuppression remission/cure 90%
Kawasaki80% <4 years

  • GPA c-ANCA 95%
  • MPA GN + capillaritis 90%
  • EGPA mononeuritis multiplex 70%
BuergerYoung males <35
Hemangioma
  • 7% of benign tumors in childhood
  • capillary regresses 75-90% at 1-3 yrs, complete by 7
Pyogenic granuloma
  • ⅓ after trauma
  • 1-2 cm
Kaposi sarcoma
  • In ⅓ of AIDS
  • HHV-8 in 95% of HIV KS
  • classic 90% older men, 10% visceral
  • African 100% mortality in 3 yrs

If you see X → think Y

  • Elderly, severe headache, tender cord-like temporal nodules, giant cells → GCA
  • Young Asian woman, weak arm pulses, bounding leg pulses → Takayasu
  • Hepatitis B patient with vasculitis → Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Child, fever, red cracked lips, cervical LAD, peeling palms, coronary ring aneurysm → Kawasaki
  • Saddle nose + cavitary lung nodules + hematuria/RPGN → GPA (Wegener)
  • Asthma + eosinophilia + vasculitis → Churg-Strauss (EGPA)
  • Young male smoker + gangrene + thrombus with microabscesses → Buerger
  • PTU → p-ANCA (MPO)
  • Strawberry red infant lesion that regresses → capillary hemangioma
  • Painful red-blue subungual nodule → glomus tumor
  • Milky fluid cystic mass, neck/axilla of child → cystic hygroma
  • Port wine stain on trigeminal area + seizures + intellectual disability → Sturge-Weber
  • Spider angioma + cirrhosis or pregnancy → hyperestrogenic state
  • AD telangiectasias of lips + epistaxis → HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu)
  • Purple skin plaques + HIV → Epidemic (AIDS) KS
  • Arsenic, thorotrast, PVC, post-mastectomy lymphedema → Angiosarcoma (CD31, vWF)
Common exam traps
  • PAN is NOT ANCA associated and spares pulmonary arteries.
  • PAN lesions are at different stages, MPA lesions are the same age.
  • GCA and Takayasu look alike histologically: distinguish by age and clinical correlation.
  • GPA is c-ANCA (PR3) per Robbins, but the lecturer gave p-ANCA in the synchronous quiz.
  • Cavernous hemangioma does not regress, capillary hemangioma does.
  • Classic, African, and transplant KS are not related to HIV.
  • Vascular ectasias are not true tumors.
  • Glomus tumor arises from modified smooth muscle cells, not endothelium.
Important warnings
  • Kawasaki: leading cause of acquired heart disease in childhood (US, Japan).
  • PAN untreated is typically fatal.
  • Takayasu: associated HPN may be difficult to control, few recover completely.
  • Esophageal varices: life-threatening hemorrhage.
  • Hemangioma in the brain may be fatal.
  • Angiosarcoma: aggressive, metastasis, poor outcome.
